title: When Emotions Run Too High in the Workplace
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece distinguishes between the biological, inborn capacity for emotion and the learned, culturally shaped ways people express it, arguing the second part is always within a person's control. It rejects the idea that some people are simply hardwired to yell or overreact, framing emotional expression as a skill that can be calibrated. The piece warns that organizations which tolerate extreme emotional displays get more of them over time, which erodes candor and openness. It closes urging leaders to hold 'respect' as a higher workplace value than unrestrained 'self-expression.'
points: The capacity for emotion is biological, but how it's expressed is learned and can be regulated.
No one is destined by upbringing or 'blood' to have a short fuse — people always retain a choice in how they respond.
Organizations that tolerate outbursts or sulking normalize and get more of that behavior.
Tolerating extreme emotionality makes team members afraid to give candid feedback, so they go quiet instead.
quotes: Infants across cultures show similar emotions of fear, joy, anger, sadness, and surprise when exposed to the same stimuli.
While the capacity for emotion is inborn, how emotions are understood, expressed, and managed is very much learned.
Since the expression of emotions is learned, people always have the ability to calibrate their responses.
When people are rewarded for becoming overly emotional, they will double down on inappropriate expression.
Leaders and workplaces that tolerate extreme and inappropriate emotionality get a lot more of it.
Insist on holding the value of respect higher than the value of self-expression.
